about: A neighbourhood cat and its feeders

lines.text: Nobody knows exactly when the orange cat first appeared at the void deck
of Block 12. It simply arrived one evening and choose a spot beside
lines.note: Tense: 'arrived … and chose' — both verbs are in the past.

lines.text: the letterboxes. Residents soon named the cat Biscuit because of it sandy colour.
lines.note: Pronoun: the colour belongs to the cat, so it is 'its'.

lines.text: Since then, an elderly man from the third floor have fed it every
lines.note: Agreement: 'an elderly man' is one person, so it is 'has fed'.

lines.text: morning before he goes to the market. Other neighbours leave bowls of water
and have even paid for the cat to be examine by a vet.
lines.note: Verb form: after 'to be' it is 'examined'.

lines.text: Not everyone is pleased, however. A few resident complain that stray animals bring
fleas and dirt. To settle the matter peaceful, the neighbours met and made
lines.note: Word form: 'settle' is a verb, so it takes the adverb 'peacefully'.

lines.text: a few rules. Food must be placed in one corner, but the bowls
lines.note: Connector: this is a second rule, not a contrast, so it is 'and'.

lines.text: must be washed daily. Biscuit, that seems unaware of the fuss, still sleeps
lines.note: Relative pronoun: after a comma it is 'which' (or 'who' for a pet), never 'that'.

lines.text: on the same step every afternoon. Children stop to stroke it on their
way home, and even the unhappy neighbours have begun to smile.
